🍎 Lesson plan · 🌍 AI in your world · Lesson 13

Lesson plan: Data: The Fuel of AI

Where the examples that AI learns from come from, how they go wrong, and why a model is always tested on examples it has never seen.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain where training data and labels come from, including the people who label it;
  • find common problems in a dataset (missing, wrong, repeated and impossible values) and say why they matter;
  • explain why a model is tested on a test set it never learned from, and recognise overfitting.

Warm-up

Your phone suggests the next word as you type. Where did it learn which word usually comes next?

Collect answers on the board (books, websites, your own messages...). Point out that every answer is a kind of data, and ask who decided what went into it.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Data: The Fuel of AI”. Students look for three ways data is collected, four kinds of messy data, and what a test set is for.

Activity: Mini-lab “Data detective”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 13 and read the table before tapping anything.
  2. In pairs, they write down which rows they think are broken, and why.
  3. They tap the rows and read each explanation, until all four problems are found.
  4. They fill in the worksheet's table, then discuss: what would a model learn from each problem if nobody fixed it?

For students who finish early

Fast finishers open “Grow a decision tree” in the AI Lab, choose “Cycling days”, and compare a tree 2 levels deep with one 6 levels deep: which is better on new days, and why?

Discussion questions

  • Many people who label data for AI are paid very little. Should users of AI care? Why?
  • A face dataset has mostly photos of one group of people. Who might the model work worse for?
  • Is it fair for an app to use what you clicked to train its AI? What would make it fair?
  • Why can a model be 99% right on its training data and still be bad?

Exit ticket

In one sentence, explain why a model is tested on examples it has never seen.

Quick check. A model scores 99% on its training data but only 60% on new data. What most likely happened?
Right answer: It overfitted: it memorised details of the training data instead of the general rule

Easier and harder

Easier. Before the mini-lab, show a short class list on the board with one obvious mistake (a 150-year-old student) and find it together.

Harder. Students design a small dataset of their own (8 rows about a school topic), hide three problems in it, and swap it with another pair to clean.
